1.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, put forth a riddle, and speak a parable unto the house of Israel; And say, Thus saith the Lord God; A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar: He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants. He took also of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful field; he placed it by great waters, and set it as a willow tree. And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs. There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers: and, behold, this vine did bend her roots toward him, and shot forth her branches toward him, that he might water it by the furrows of her plantation. It was planted in a good soil by great waters, that it might bring forth branches, and that it might bear fruit, that it might be a goodly vine. Say thou, Thus saith the Lord God; Shall it prosper? shall he not pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it wither? it shall wither in all the leaves of her spring, even without great power or many people to pluck it up by the roots thereof. Yea, behold, being planted, shall it prosper? shall it not utterly wither, when the east wind toucheth it? it shall wither in the furrows where it grew.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter in three, parable, interpretation applied to Zedekiah, and closing promise; Ellicott notes the definite article before the eagle, derives its variegated plumage from an empire of differing languages and customs, takes the mountain for Jerusalem since the cedar belongs there and the palace was named for its forest of cedar, observes that the Hebrew calls the merchant land a land of Canaan, a word used elsewhere for merchandise and already applied to that city for its trade, gives the second eagle no variegated feathers since he ruled no such medley of peoples, and renders the closing threat to say that not even great power will raise the plant from its roots again.

Gill sets the occasion, a people charged with breaking faith with God now charged with breaking faith with men, hears a whetting in the Hebrew word for riddle, dates the cropped shoot at eighteen years old and taken within three months, stresses that the substitute chosen was no stranger but one of the blood royal renamed at his patron's pleasure, and identifies the second eagle with the ruler a Greek historian calls Apries; Calvin states the burden soberly, that the Jews were fools to think themselves safe with God for an adversary, would render the command enigmatize an enigma, distinguishes obscurity that hides from the impious from obscurity that wakes the hardened, argues from greater to less about the conqueror, denies that the mountain is the city, finds an Egyptian irrigation custom behind the bending roots, and thinks the ingratitude worse in a private man raised beyond expectation.

Clarke can hardly praise the chapter enough for its images, composition and transitions, and reads the eagle clause by clause, great wings for an extensive empire, length of wing for speed of conquest, thick plumage for many subjects, varied colours for many nations, deriving the English word riddle from sifting and the Hebrew from a root meaning to pierce; Wesley reads the young twigs as the princes generally and adds that no great force is needed, a kingdom uprooted as we uproot a tree that cumbers the ground.

Henry denies any intent to baffle, since the meaning is given at once, and explains the form as chosen so that hearers will notice, feel, remember and repeat it, which is why similitudes were common with the prophets and parables with Christ.

debates.question: What is the mountain from which the top of the cedar is taken?

positions.position: Jerusalem, since the cedar belongs there and the royal palace was named for its forest of cedar.
Not the city but the land: the passage usually cited in support speaks of the temple, and the mountain is named for its trees and because the allegory needed it.

outliers.claim: Traces the English word riddle to a coarse sieve for cleaning corn and the Hebrew to a root meaning to pierce, adding that it is not what pierces the mind but what the mind must pierce.
Insists the arrangement was designed to work: a native prince rather than a satrap, a kingdom low but flourishing and useful against Egypt, which is why its frustration provoked such rage.

11.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Say now to the rebellious house, Know ye not what these things mean? tell them, Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon; And hath taken of the king’s seed, and made a covenant with him, and hath taken an oath of him: he hath also taken the mighty of the land: That the kingdom might be base, that it might not lift itself up, but that by keeping of his covenant it might stand. But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people. Shall he prosper? shall he escape that doeth such things? or shall he break the covenant, and be delivered? As I live, saith the Lord God, surely in the place where the king dwelleth that made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant he brake, even with him in the midst of Babylon he shall die. Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company make for him in the war, by casting up mounts, and building forts, to cut off many persons:

schools.summary: Ellicott thinks an interval probably separated the parable from its explanation, so that a spell of puzzlement would leave the hearers more attentive, supplies the precedent of an oath extracted by fraud from an earlier generation which still bound the nation centuries later, notes that the king had been warned more than once through Jeremiah, finds the sentence of death exactly fitted to the crime and the tense turning future, corrects the rendering that makes the siege-works Pharaoh's own since ramps and forts belong to a besieging army, and records that an Egyptian force did briefly lift the siege before the Chaldeans returned and burned the city.

Gill names the substitute as the deported king's uncle and lingers on the throne-name given him, which means the justice of the Lord and was a standing reminder to keep the covenant or expect vengeance, reads base as a viceroy paying tribute and subjects paying tax, and notes that the reply is itself an oath which the Jewish commentators mark as such; Calvin explains the riddle as designed to hold a people practised in despising rebukes, repeats that the mountain is not the city, insists the conditions were published openly and were moderate where hard ones could have been imposed, uses the divine oath to argue that we should not rush into swearing, and answers the difficulty that the man was to die in Babylon yet never saw it, his eyes having been put out at Riblah.

Clarke adds that the state was to have no political weight and would sink at last into a client governorship, narrows the date of the Egyptian embassy to the months between two of the prophet's dated visions, and states the blinding and the death in exile without treating them as a difficulty; Wesley reduces the case to a question, whether perjury can be a road to deliverance.

Henry generalises the offence: ingratitude to a benefactor is a sin against God, every solemn oath calls God to witness, truth is a debt owed to all men, and treachery is worse rather than better when the true religion deals falsely with the false.

debates.question: What does the threat about Pharaoh's forces mean?

positions.position: Not that the promised help was undersized, as kings promise fifty thousand and send ten, but that whatever was attempted would simply fail.
That the siege-works are not Pharaoh's act at all: the clause should read of the time when they are cast up, and the relieving force achieved nothing.

outliers.claim: Reads the throne-name imposed on the substitute king, which means the justice of the Lord, as itself a standing reminder to keep the covenant or expect vengeance.
Meets the objection that the man was sentenced to die in Babylon and never saw it, his eyes having been put out on the way, by taking the sentence to mean death in exile.

18.pericope_label: Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these things, he shall not escape. Therefore thus saith the Lord God; As I live, surely mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head. And I will spread my net upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon, and will plead with him there for his trespass that he hath trespassed against me. And all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword, and they that remain shall be scattered toward all winds: and ye shall know that I the Lord have spoken it.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that the sworn covenant with a foreign king is called the Lord's, both because it was made in his name and because he had required it, so that rebelling against that king was in these circumstances apostasy from God himself, and marks the boundary at the end of the interpretation, since what follows keeps the imagery but answers to nothing in either the parable or its explanation.

Gill takes the second statement of the despised oath as deliberate emphasis on the enormity and on the cause of the ruin, and reads the slaughter of those who broke out when the city fell; Calvin reads the given hand as the customary gesture by which men witnessed an agreement, explains that common convictions about the sacredness of treaties evaporate because those who hold them do not hold the point on which they depend, that God judges the world, makes the net identify capture rather than any other stroke and explains how an invading army acting on its own designs is still directed by a providence it knows nothing of, and describes how troops in formation absorb an attack while troops dispersed are each at the enemy's mercy.

Clarke says the offence is particularly resented, since the man had sworn in the divine presence and broke it at the first opportunity, and agrees that those who ran toward Egypt were cut down; Wesley notes that the given hand solemnly confirms the oath and enters the usual caution that all here means the greater part rather than every man.

outliers.claim: Argues that the general human conviction that treaties are sacred is born with us and follows nature rather than faith, so that it evaporates unless the specific declaration names God as the avenger.
Holds that rebellion against the foreign king was apostasy from God, because the oath was sworn in his name and at his command.

22.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent: In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell. And all the trees of the field shall know that I the Lord have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the Lord have spoken and have done it.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch put it briefly, that the sovereignty is lost through breach of faith while the kingdom is not; Ellicott marks the change of agent from a foreign king pursuing his own ends to God acting directly, holds that the allegory requires a historical person whom the description allows to be only one, notes that the word for tender bears on lowliness of origin, contrasts the goodly cedar with the low vine of the parable, identifies the mountain with Zion while warning against pressing the literal hill, draws out the principle that the later dispensation is rooted in the earlier, and sets the closing reversal beside the two songs that celebrate the same overturning.

Gill states the fear the promise answers, that the tribe was lost and the pledge of a perpetual throne void, and reports the Jewish opinion that the land stood higher than all others and the city highest in it; Calvin refuses to collapse the return and the later kingdom into one, warns that Christian writers who insist all such language means Christ alone make themselves ridiculous to Jewish readers, dates the reign from the rebuilding of the temple after the seventy years and runs it to the last day, observes that cedars grow slowly so that a twig becoming a great tree exceeds the ordinary rule of nature, and resolves the contradiction between plucking a twig from a lofty cedar and raising what was low by the two states of one person.

Clarke expects a monarchy in the same line, a tender plant in its incarnation and eminent afterward, turns the tree into an inventory of boughs for apostles, fruit for converts, birds for all nations and shade for saving trust, and reads the closing reversal as four specific reigns while reporting another commentator who takes high and green for the conqueror and low and dry for the conquered; Wesley calls the eminence spiritual rather than splendid, promises peace and safety in the shade, and makes the high tree the empire itself.

Henry answers the objection that the covenant of royalty had failed by calling the pledge conditional and forfeited by a posterity that broke its terms, yet not cancelled, since human unbelief does not invalidate a divine promise and another seed will be found in which it holds, allowing a partial fulfilment in the man who led the return.

debates.question: What are the trees of the field in the closing reversal?

positions.position: Four specific reigns: a king dethroned, his successor raised, that successor dried when his sons were killed, and a dry stock made to flourish in the promised heir.
The empire itself, brought low at last by its own conquerors.
All other earthly powers, which must finally acknowledge the work of God in redemption.
All the kings of the earth and everyone possessed of dignity.

debates.question: How far does the promise reach?

positions.position: From the rebuilding of the temple after the seventy years through the whole progress of the kingdom to the last day, not to one person only.
A partial fulfilment in the leader of the return, the full one later.
To one historical person whom the description allows to be only the Messiah.

outliers.claim: Warns that Christian writers who insist everything said about restoring the Church must mean Christ alone make themselves ridiculous to Jewish readers, since the prophets begin at the return from exile.
Reports a rival identification of the trees on which the high and green tree is the conqueror and the low and dry tree the conquered people.

themes: Thus saith the Lord God; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:

In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell.

And all the trees of the field shall know that I the Lord have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the Lord have spoken and have done it.
